alpha-centauri.title: Alpha Centauri
alpha-centauri.info: The nearest star system to Earth — three suns: a Sun-like yellow dwarf (the Na'vi Tsawke), an orange dwarf, and distant red Proxima. Pandora orbits Polyphemus, which orbits Alpha Centauri A. Click a star to read its card.

habitable-zone.title: Habitable Zone
habitable-zone.info: The band of distances around a star where liquid water can persist — not too hot, not too cold. A brighter star pushes the zone outward. Drag the stellar mass to see Pandora drift in and out of the green band.

exomoon.title: Exomoon
exomoon.info: A moon orbiting a planet in another star system. A habitable exomoon balances four heat sources — direct starlight, reflected planetshine, the giant's infrared glow, and internal tidal heat. Shrink the orbit and tidal heating climbs.

roche-limit.title: Roche Limit
roche-limit.info: The closest a moon can approach before the planet's tidal force overpowers the moon's own gravity and tears it apart into a debris ring. Drag the moon inward past the limit and watch it disrupt.

accretion.title: Accretion
accretion.info: How planets and moons grow — by sweeping up dust and gas from a surrounding disk. Raise the collapse rate and watch hundreds of particles spiral inward and coalesce into a young protoplanet.

planetary-differentiation.title: Planetary Differentiation
planetary-differentiation.info: A molten young world separates by density — heavy metal sinks to form a core, lighter rock rises to mantle and crust. Scrub through time to watch the layers sort themselves.

biosignature.title: Biosignature
biosignature.info: The strongest atmospheric sign of life is not one gas but the coexistence of gases that should destroy each other — like O₂ and CH₄. They persist together only if life keeps replenishing them. Toggle gases on a dead vs living world and watch the disequilibrium glow.

direct-imaging.title: Direct Imaging
direct-imaging.info: The hardest planet-hunting method: capture the planet's own light by hiding the star's glare behind an occulting disk (a coronagraph). Slide the occulter into place and watch the star vanish, revealing a faint planet in the cleared dark.

radial-velocity.title: Radial Velocity
radial-velocity.info: A star and its planet both orbit a shared centre of mass, so the star sways. Toward us its light shifts bluer, away redder — the Doppler wobble. Read the rhythmic colour-shift to get the planet's period and minimum mass.

transmission-spectroscopy.title: Transmission Spectroscopy
transmission-spectroscopy.info: As a planet crosses its star, a sliver of starlight strains through its atmosphere. Each gas absorbs at characteristic wavelengths, leaving dark fingerprint lines in the spectrum. Toggle molecules to see their absorption bands appear.

transit-timing-variation.title: Transit-Timing Variation
transit-timing-variation.info: A moon tugs its planet around their shared centre of mass, so the planet transits its star a little early or late each orbit. Drag the hidden moon and watch the lightcurve dip shift — the fingerprint of an unseen body.

tidal-heating.title: Tidal Heating
tidal-heating.info: On an off-circular orbit a moon is squeezed harder when close, less when far — that rhythmic flexing heats its interior by friction. It drives Io's volcanoes and Pandora's geology. Raise the eccentricity and the core glows hotter.

faint-young-sun-paradox.title: Faint Young Sun Paradox
faint-young-sun-paradox.info: Four billion years ago the Sun shone about 30% dimmer, yet the rocks record liquid water, not a frozen snowball. Scrub through deep time: the faint-sun curve drops the surface into the ice band — until you switch on the carbonate-silicate thermostat and a thicker CO₂ greenhouse holds the world warm.

gyrochronology.title: Gyrochronology
gyrochronology.info: A low-mass star is a clock you can read by its spin. Young stars whirl fast and bright; over billions of years magnetic winds bleed off angular momentum and the spin slows predictably. Drag the age and watch the starspots crawl slower and the glow cool — the rotation period gives the age.

libration.title: Libration
libration.info: A tidally locked moon shows one face on average — but an off-circular orbit and a tilted axis make it slowly rock and nod, letting you peek over each limb in turn. That wobble is why we see 59% of the Moon, not half. Toggle libration off to freeze the face dead still.

obliquity.title: Obliquity
obliquity.info: Seasons come from axial tilt, not distance from the star. Whichever hemisphere leans sunward catches more direct light and runs warm; the other tilts into winter and grows ice. Drag the tilt from upright to steep and watch the polar caps and seasons swing.

orbital-resonance.title: Orbital Resonance
orbital-resonance.info: When moons fall into simple whole-number period ratios they tug each other at the same points every orbit, locking into a rhythm — like Io, Europa, and Ganymede at 4:2:1. The periodic kicks keep their orbits eccentric and feed tidal heat. Pick a ratio and watch the traced pattern lock clean or dissolve into chaos.

planetshine.title: Planetshine
planetshine.info: Sunlight bouncing off a giant planet floods its moon's night side — the same trick that makes the dark of a young crescent Moon faintly glow (earthshine). Polyphemus is so vast and bright that Pandora's planet-facing night rarely goes truly dark. Toggle the reflected light and watch the bioluminescent world brighten.

sidereal-day.title: Sidereal Day
sidereal-day.info: A sidereal day is one true 360° spin measured against the distant stars. But while the world turns it also moves along its orbit, so it must rotate a little further to bring the sun back overhead — that extra turn is the solar day. Step through the orbit and watch the two day-marks drift apart.

spin-orbit-resonance.title: Spin-Orbit Resonance
spin-orbit-resonance.info: A whole-number lock between how often a world spins and how often it orbits. Tidal locking is the 1:1 case; Mercury is trapped at 3:2 — three spins for every two orbits — because its orbit is so eccentric. Switch ratios and watch the surface marker trace its signature petal path.

synchronous-rotation.title: Synchronous Rotation
synchronous-rotation.info: The result of tidal locking: a moon spins exactly once per orbit, so the same hemisphere always faces its host. It does NOT mean one side is forever dark — the moon still turns relative to the star, so it still has day and night. Toggle to break the lock and let the far side rotate into view.

synodic-day.title: Synodic Day
synodic-day.info: The synodic (solar) day is sunrise to sunrise — the day we actually live by — and it runs a touch longer than the true sidereal spin. On Pandora, locked to Polyphemus, the giant hangs fixed in the sky and the sun ducks behind it: an eclipse marks the rhythm of each day. Step through to flag the eclipse events.

tidal-locking.title: Tidal Locking
tidal-locking.info: Gravity stretches a moon into an egg shape; friction in that tidal bulge brakes its spin until rotation matches the orbit and one face stays turned toward the host forever. The Moon locked to Earth this way; Pandora locked to Polyphemus, so its day equals its month. Speed the spin and watch it brake into lock.
